description: The single source of truth for every numeric budget the app is gated on, except the renderer bundle sizes, which size-limit checks against the budgets in `apps/desktop/.size-limit.ts`. Rows carry a `scope`. A `product` row is one of the app's own product figures, written here whether or not this revision can measure it, because a budget silently omitted is a budget nobody notices is ungated. A `harness` row is a bound the scaffolding applies to itself or to what the endurance tier reads off the app, with no product figure behind it, so its `specTarget` states the bound in its own terms while `harnessBudgetDerivation` states, once for the whole set, why those figures and not others. Both kinds live here for the same reason: one value, one home. An entry whose `status` is "n/a" is not measurable at this revision and names, in `notMeasurableReason`, what is missing.
harnessBudgetDerivation: A `harness` row has no product figure behind it, so this field says, once for the whole set, where its number comes from; a derivation copied into each row would have as many places to drift as there are rows. There are two groups. THE FIVE `launch-*` AND `endurance-body` ROWS are the slices of ONE tier timeout. Three bound the launch: `tests/helpers/launch/deadline.ts` mints one deadline per launch and divides it into readiness, the frame paint probe and cleanup, so a launch that overruns produces its own diagnostic instead of Vitest's undiagnosable kill. The other two bound the caller's test body between a settled launch and its cleanup, so Vitest never kills a body mid-poll, before the poll's own message or the cleanup settles, leaving an Electron alive. A launching tier's `testTimeout` is derived from these rows rather than written as a literal: `tierTimeoutFor()` in `tests/helpers/launch/deadline.ts` sums the launch budget, the body allowance that tier applies, and a 2 000 ms settlement residual — a floor rather than a ceiling, which is why it is a constant beside these rows and not a row among them, since every row here is a ceiling. The `launch-cleanup` row is reserved TWICE inside the launch budget (`CLEANUP_PHASES` in `tests/helpers/launch/deadline.ts`), because one cleanup spends it in two phases: the close it races, and then the termination loop that restarts the same figure when the close had to be abandoned. The body allowance is per tier because the two tiers' bodies are different subjects — a driven interaction against a sustained workload — and a tier that states none gets the shorter one, so a new tier fails inside its own bound rather than quietly under Vitest's. The figures are generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case these must not flake on, and each is a ceiling for a wedged phase rather than an expectation. THE FOUR ENDURANCE DETECTION ROWS (`steady-heap-growth`, `detached-node-retention`, `transcript-fold-cost-ratio` and `transcript-fold-retention`) bound what the endurance tier reads off the app over a workload no product figure names: a growth, a retention or a cost ratio rather than a product ceiling. Each sits below what the defect it hunts would produce and above the noise a clean run carries, and its row's `notes` says how.
enduranceTierNotGatedReason: Every row the endurance tier's harnesses measure is `n/a` for one shared reason, stated here once rather than copied into each row: the tier runs only by name (`test:endurance`). It is in no CI job and outside the aggregate `test` script until the endurance reference run makes it a gate on every PR. Each such row's `notMeasurableReason` names its harness and the symbol that harness holds, and points here.

unitConventions.MB: 1000000 bytes (SI). The spec writes `MB`; the SI reading is also the stricter one (120 MB = 120000000 B, against 120 MiB = 125829120 B), so taking it costs the budget nothing and cannot make a passing measurement out of a failing one.
unitConventions.MiB: 1048576 bytes (binary). The spec writes `MiB` for the terminal budget explicitly, so this one is not an interpretation.
unitConventions.ratio: a plain quotient of two readings taken in the same unit
unitConventions.percentOfOneCore: percent of a single core, averaged over the window the budget's `specTarget` names

measurementProtocol.deterministic: Heap at rest, steady heap, and first-transcript-row latency against the fixture's frozen clock gate on any runner.
measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent: Frame time and CPU are measured from the built bundle running in Electron against the fixture bridge's concurrent-streaming scenario with the frozen clock, ten warm-up seconds discarded, the metric taken as the median of three runs, on the pinned CI runner class the desktop workflow names by label, with thresholds calibrated on that class at first landing with 25 % headroom and one automatic re-run before a failure counts.
measurementProtocol.referenceProfile: The `limit` figures are the product targets on the laptop-class reference profile — eight cores, integrated GPU, one 60 Hz display. The runner-calibrated thresholds are stated apart from them, so a runner regression and a product regression stay distinguishable.

budgets.label: Frame time, four lanes streaming
budgets.subject: The 95th-percentile frame duration of the renderer while four agent lanes stream concurrently into the transcript, measured from the built bundle running in Electron against the fixture bridge's concurrent-streaming scenario with the frozen clock. The concurrency is a property of the sampled window rather than a description of it: the harness reads the peak number of runs mid-turn inside its own window off the scenario's beats and fails when it is not one lane per attached agent.
budgets.specTarget: p95 ≤ 16.7 ms on the reference machine
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/frame-time.test.ts` measures it, through `sampleFrameTimings`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: the harness compares it on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`. Off that class the harness still runs and prints the figure — the instrument is exercised everywhere and the comparison is withheld — which `tests/endurance/pinned-runner-class.ts` decides for the whole tier. The reading is the median of three fresh launches' p95, each sampling 300 frame durations with a warm-up discarded, taken by nearest rank. A frame's duration runs from the start of its `requestAnimationFrame` callback to the first task that runs after that frame's rendering has been committed, which is the main-thread work the frame cost. It is not the interval between frames: an interval is bounded below by the display's own refresh period, so on the 60 Hz reference profile it reads ~16.7 ms for a renderer doing nothing and could never be under this ceiling. The warm-up is a frame count rather than the protocol's ten seconds because a frozen clock walked for ten seconds would deliver the whole script before the first sample. No runner-calibrated threshold is recorded yet, so the comparison is against this row's own product limit. The concurrent-streaming scenario drives four runs mid-turn at the same tick with interleaved thinking, message and tool beats, an approval blocking one lane while the other three keep talking, a cost reading per lane, and a helper run threaded to the turn that spawned it. The run asserts three things about its own sampled window rather than describing them — the script finished delivering inside it, it was still arriving during it, and four lanes were streaming inside it, the last read off the scenario's beats by `tests/endurance/streaming-lanes.ts` and checked against the scenario's own cast size. Measured on an eight-core laptop across three passes of the tier: per-run p95 6.80–9.20 ms beside a p50 of 0.10–0.20 ms. Both statistics are printed, because a p50 sitting at the display's refresh period is the cadence being reported rather than the app's work. The spread is recorded rather than a single figure pinned, because a duration is a property of the machine's CPU as much as of the app — the same fact that keeps the comparison on the pinned runner class.

budgets.label: Renderer heap, one session open at rest
budgets.subject: Retained JavaScript heap with one session open and nothing streaming — the app's stores, projections, and persistence layer settled, after a forced garbage collection.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/heap/at-rest.test.ts` measures it, through `RendererHeapProbe`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Deliberately NOT measured in a Node process: a Node reading holds no Chromium, no renderer isolate, no React, no DOM and no app store, so it could report green over a renderer well past 120 MB, which is the one failure a budget exists to catch. The endurance tier launches the built app, opens the concurrent-streaming scenario's own session, walks the frozen clock over the whole script, asserts the store admitted events through a live subscription, and reads `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` behind a forced collection over a DevTools session, as the minimum over settling samples. The forced collection matters because the precision precondition this tier runs before every gated reading allocates four megabytes and drops them, and a sampler that collects nothing can carry them into the figure the ceiling is compared against. That figure counts allocated-and-not-yet-collected bytes, so it sits at or above the retained heap this row bounds, which is the safe direction for a ceiling. The reading is a renderer isolate figure taken in the built app in unobtrusive-window mode; the substrate floor with no session content measures 6,564,912 B.

budgets.label: Steady heap, concurrent-streaming live stream
budgets.subject: Renderer heap over thirty minutes of the concurrent-streaming scenario streaming live on the scenario clock — both its ceiling and its slope, since a heap that stays under the ceiling while climbing monotonically is still a leak.
budgets.specTarget: flat over thirty minutes; ≤ 250 MB renderer heap
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/heap/instrument.ts` forces a collection over a CDP `HeapProfiler` session, `steady-state.test.ts` bounds heap GROWTH across 200 churn cycles that stream the in-tree concurrent-streaming script through the fixture bridge once, and `endurance/heap/at-rest.test.ts` measures the at-rest ceiling when the endurance tier is run by name — and none of the three conditions THIS row states is met by those. No run holds the app for thirty minutes: the `endurance-body` allowance is nine. No snapshot SERIES is analyzed for slope: `endurance/heap/snapshot-analysis.ts` reads a single snapshot by constructor with `memlab`, which answers what one heap is holding rather than whether a run's heap climbed, so the flat-over-thirty-minutes criterion has no verdict behind it. And there is no dated endurance record to log a refutation in.
budgets.notes: Not wired: no task yet holds the app for thirty minutes and reads its heap for slope.

budgets.label: Idle CPU, session open, nothing streaming
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer with a session open and no stream running, averaged over sixty seconds — together with the assertion that no timer fires in that window except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 0.5 % of one core averaged over sixty seconds; no timer fires except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat
budgets.notMeasurableReason: No harness on any tier samples renderer CPU, so the sixty-second average is not taken. The criterion beside it is not taken either: it names what FIRED inside that window, and no tier watches a running renderer's timers — `no-restricted-globals` in `eslint.config.mjs` refuses `setInterval` in renderer source, which is the different claim this row's notes already distinguish. The subject is in tree — the endurance tier opens the concurrent-streaming session route in the built app and `lib/reads/refresh/scheduler.ts` owns every refresh — so what is missing is the instrument, which the endurance reference run still owes.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`. The timer-enumeration half is a lint rule (`no-restricted-globals` on `setInterval`, in `eslint.config.mjs`), not a number.

budgets.label: Streaming CPU, one lane
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer while one agent lane streams into the transcript, together with the assertion that the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent rather than overrunning it.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 % of one core on the reference machine; the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent
budgets.notMeasurableReason: No harness on any tier samples renderer CPU. The subject is in tree — the concurrent-streaming scenario drives four lanes, `tests/endurance/streaming-lanes.ts` counts them, and `frame-time.test.ts` measures a window it asserts they were streaming inside — so what is missing is the instrument, which the endurance reference run still owes.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`.

budgets.label: Terminal instance
budgets.subject: Retained memory of one `terminal` pane instance at the default scrollback — the `@xterm/xterm` instance, its WebGL renderer, and the pane's own state.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/terminal/instance/memory.test.ts` measures it, through `RendererHeapProbe`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Measured in the endurance tier: `app/pane-harness/PaneHarnessScreen.tsx` is a `define`-gated fixture view, reached at `#/pane-harness/<paneKind>/<sessionId>`, that resolves the body through the app's own `PaneRegistry` and mounts one more instance per press. So the subject is held WHOLE — the built app in a real Electron window, a `terminal` pane the registry resolved, mounted through a real React commit, its emulator on a live WebGL2 context, bound to a session the scenario engine has delivered into — and each of those is asserted rather than assumed: the run FAILS on a `dom` renderer reading rather than measuring the fallback, and fails on an empty session store rather than folding a lease off an empty log. A harness that constructed the adapter under happy-dom and sampled the Node process's own heap would measure a subject narrower than this row's sentence and could report green over a pane well past the ceiling. WHAT THE HARNESS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT HOLD is the pane area around the pane: no tab strip, no layout, no drag target, no detach path. That is closer to this row's sentence than a reading inside the pane area would be — the ceiling is per INSTANCE, and a figure taken there would fold the pane area's own cost into it and report a pane over budget for chrome the row does not name. The figure is the difference between the settled renderer heap with no instance open and with one, taken as the minimum over settling samples, after a warm-up cycle that moves the emulator chunk's one-time cost to the left of the baseline; two further instances are then opened and their per-instance slope is required to agree with that figure, which is the control against a fixed cost being reported as the instance. The adapter-level claims that ARE reachable in a Node process — scrollback eviction, disposal, and a working day of pane churn — stay on `tests/endurance/terminal/adapter.test.ts` beside the churn accounting they belong with; that file makes NO ceiling claim of its own, so neither half of the instance ever receives an independent allowance. WHAT THE FIGURE COVERS: the instance is priced as ONE populated pane — the mounted pane's standing cost plus a full buffer at the default scrollback, both measured at one width (`TERMINAL_BUDGET_MEASUREMENT_COLUMNS`) and one depth (`TERMINAL_DEFAULT_SCROLLBACK_LINES`, both in the terminal feature's `caps.ts`) and summed before a single `evaluateBudget` call. Measured on macOS: 16,456 kB of 20,480 kB (80.4 %) — pane 940 kB plus scrollback 15,516 kB at 10,000 lines × 120 columns; later panes 823 kB each; 417 kB still held after three closed; a second run reproduced the sum within 10 kB. That headroom is thin on purpose: the next thing that grows a terminal pane moves this figure, and changing either constant changes what the row means. WHAT IT CANNOT YET: the scrollback half is driven in the driver process, because the byte stream, the scrollback, and the resize report have no registered wire yet, so nothing can put a line into a MOUNTED pane — so the sum is conservative (it omits nothing the mounted pane holds and adds the buffer the pane would hold), and when that wire lands the harness drives bytes into the mounted pane and the two halves collapse into one delta. The readings are taken behind a forced collection over a DevTools session rather than from the sampler alone: a difference of a few hundred kilobytes is decided by WHEN the collector ran, and without it the same code measures a first instance at 4,165 kB and a per-instance slope of minus 5,765 kB.

budgets.label: Time to first transcript row on launch
budgets.subject: Elapsed time from window show to the first transcript row painted, in fixture mode against the frozen clock.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 800 ms from window show, fixture mode
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/first-transcript-row.test.ts` measures it, through `measureFirstTranscriptRow`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Deterministic against the fixture's frozen clock, so the harness compares it on any runner once the transcript exists — it is not one of the two hardware-dependent budgets. Window show is read as the renderer's own `first-contentful-paint` entry: main reveals the window as it adopts the window's document, before that document draws, so until that paint the window shows only its painted ground, and on macOS an automated launch deliberately never reveals the window at all — so there is no `show` timestamp to read and no wall clock is read in either process. The interval ends at the animation frame after the first row element is laid out, and the whole of it is measured inside one page function, so the only harness cost inside it is the gap between the launch handshake settling and that function starting, which the report prints separately rather than subtracting. Measured 43–46 ms of an 800 ms ceiling on an eight-core laptop across three runs of the tier, 13–22 ms of it that handshake.

budgets.label: App launch readiness ladder
budgets.subject: Wall time from `_electron.launch()` to the renderer's frame element being present — the whole cold-start ladder (the console document, its `load`, the window it opens, the frame selector) charged once between its phases rather than once each.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 30 000 ms across every readiness phase combined
budgets.notes: The whole cold-start ladder — first window, `load`, the frame selector — charged once between its phases rather than once each. Generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case it must not flake on. The derivation these bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Applied by `LaunchDeadline`, which every launching tier draws its readiness phase from.

budgets.label: App launch first-frame paint probe
budgets.subject: The wait, after the renderer reports ready, for the first animation frame to arrive — the reading that separates a window that painted from one that merely opened.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 000 ms from readiness, not from launch
budgets.notes: Armed only once readiness has landed, so a slow boot is charged to the readiness row rather than reported as a frame that never came. What it answers is whether the window painted at all, and late is not the same as never: it fails only on never. First-frame LATENCY is bounded by nothing here — `frame-time-p95-four-lanes` is `enforced` and does catch a frame-schedule regression, but its subject is the p95 of a streaming window rather than the first paint, and it compares only on the pinned runner class — so a green paint probe is a claim about paint and never about how long the paint took. The derivation these bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Applied by `FramePaintProbe`, which every launch runs once readiness lands.

budgets.label: App launch cleanup
budgets.subject: The bound `application.close()` is raced against before the Electron process tree is SIGKILLed and the temporary profile removed.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 10 000 ms, or the tree is terminated
budgets.notes: A ceiling rather than a target: what it guards against is an Electron wedged rather than slow, so what matters is that some finite number is enforced. It is the WHOLE applied bound and the same one on both closing paths — a close reached from a failed launch is held to it exactly as one reached minutes later on the success path is, so the figure a budget audit reads is the figure the harness enforces. Because `terminated` records and passes, this figure decides when the process tree is SIGKILLed rather than whether the tier goes red; `unterminable` and `closed-after-rejection` fail, and those are the two settlements that harm the launches after them. The derivation these bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Applied by `BoundedCleanup`, which races every close against it.

budgets.label: App launch test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time a test body gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — the interval `withLaunchedApp` runs the caller's own function in, and the default for a tier that states no allowance of its own.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 80 500 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: Counted from the worst body in the tree rather than chosen, with every wait in that body drawing on this allowance. `e2e/several-windows.test.ts` declares, in order: a 10 000 ms `expect.poll` for the window layout the console keeps; the reload, whose navigation, the windows it reopens and their frame elements share ONE 30 000 ms clock, because the renderer boot they perform between them is the same subject `launch-readiness` bounds; closing one window and minimizing another, 10 000 ms each; a 500 ms frame count; and two 10 000 ms `expect.poll` waits, on the View menu's scheme reaching each window still open — 20 000 ms in all. 10 000 + 30 000 + 20 000 + 500 + 20 000 is this figure. A bound under a body's own declared waits would fire first and replace that body's message ("the scheme did not change") with a sentence about a clock, which is the inversion the launch deadline exists to undo. A body is handed what is LEFT of this allowance and asks for `boundedMs(<its own bound>)`, the smaller of the two, so the first wait that cannot fit fails with ITS sentence rather than the generic overrun. That every bounded wait in a launching tier draws on the allowance is a reviewer's check — `apps/desktop/AGENTS.md` states it — rather than a source scan. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Applied by `BodyAllowance`, which every launching tier's body draws on.

budgets.label: App endurance test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time the endurance tier's sustained workload gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — hundreds of driven churn cycles and the settling heap samples either side of them.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 540 000 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: A separate figure because the endurance body is a different subject from an end-to-end one, not a slower version of it: `steady-state.test.ts` drives 200 churn cycles twice over with settling heap samples either side, which its own count comment measures at roughly 50 ms a cycle — well under a minute warm, and the reason that tier carries a patience an order of magnitude past the end-to-end one. Nine minutes puts the derived tier timeout at 607 000 ms, which is `tierTimeoutFor(540 000)` read off its own constants: `LAUNCH_BUDGET_MS` of 65 000 — 30 000 readiness plus 15 000 frame paint probe plus `CLEANUP_PHASES` × 10 000 cleanup — then this allowance, then the 2 000 ms settlement residual. Its own waits draw on this allowance through the same `boundedMs` the end-to-end bodies use, but this FIGURE is deliberately not counted from them: a churn cycle's declared bounds are ceilings for a wedged app rather than intervals a run spends, and 200 of them summed would describe no run this tier performs. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`.

budgets.label: Steady-state heap growth across route churn
budgets.subject: How much the renderer heap grows between the settled reading after warm-up and the settled reading after the endurance tier's churn cycles over the concurrent-streaming workload, each behind a forced collection.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 8 MiB of growth across the run
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/steady-state.test.ts` measures it, through `RendererHeapProbe`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Not zero, because V8 keeps caches, code objects and deoptimization data alive across a run. Not a percentage, because a percentage of a large baseline is a large absolute allowance and a leak's size does not depend on the application's. Over the run's 200 cycles a leak of about 40 kB a cycle reaches it; a smaller leak is below what this instrument can see. It bounds a difference of two readings, never the heap itself: the ceiling at rest is `renderer-heap-at-rest`'s and the thirty-minute slope is `steady-heap-concurrent-streaming`'s, so no number has two owners.

budgets.label: Detached DOM retained across route churn
budgets.subject: The bytes the renderer heap retains in `Detached HTMLDivElement` nodes after a quarter of `steady-heap-growth`'s churn cycles, read by constructor from one heap snapshot taken behind a forced collection.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 4 MiB of detached nodes after the churn
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/steady-state.test.ts` measures it, through `RendererHeapProbe`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Well above the transient detachment a React unmount leaves for the next collection and far below a frame that retained one route's subtree per cycle; at this many cycles the smallest per-cycle retention it can see is about 80 kB, and a clean run on macOS reads 0 kB. Not derived from `steady-heap-growth`: that bounds a difference of two readings over the whole application, this an absolute retention of one constructor. The same snapshot's `Map`, `Array` and attached `HTMLDivElement` readings are its controls, so a snapshot that was never parsed, or that spells DOM nodes differently, fails instead of reading zero.

budgets.label: Transcript fold cost over a four times longer log
budgets.subject: How many times longer the transcript's fold, `deriveTranscriptWindow`, takes over a generated ten-thousand-row session than over a quarter of it, each the fastest of several passes.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 8 times the cost for a log four times as long
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/transcript/long-log.test.ts` measures it, through `deriveTranscriptWindow`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: A ratio between two sizes rather than a wall-clock ceiling, so a slower machine does not break it. The step is four times, so a linear fold lands near 4 and a quadratic one near 16. Measured at about 4.4 (2,500 rows fold in ~2.5 ms, 10,000 in ~11 ms, best of five on an eight-core laptop); 8 leaves room over noise while sitting half way to the quadratic figure. Fixed per-call overhead can only push the ratio down, so it cannot manufacture a failure.

budgets.label: Transcript fold retention
budgets.subject: What twenty folds of a generated ten-thousand-row session add to the heap of the process running the fold, `deriveTranscriptWindow`, read behind a forced collection.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: `tests/endurance/transcript/long-log.test.ts` measures it, through `deriveTranscriptWindow`, when the endurance tier is run by name (`test:endurance`). Why that tier gates nothing yet is stated once in `enduranceTierNotGatedReason`.
budgets.notes: Not zero, because V8 keeps code objects, inline caches and deoptimization data alive across a run. Not a fraction of the baseline, since a leak's size does not depend on how large the process was. Bounded from both sides: one held window over this log measures ~3.9 MB, so a ceiling above that could not catch a fold keeping a single one of its twenty outputs; 2 MiB sits under one window and two orders of magnitude above the ~21 kB twenty clean folds retain. A Node heap reading is honest here because the subject is the fold's own retained structures, which live in whatever process runs it; it states no renderer ceiling.
